newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Rifkind says Jewish settlements illegal.
newsitem.headline: Rifkind says Jewish settlements illegal.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Sunday Jewish settlements in Arab occupied territories were illegal and should not continue.
Voicing a long-held British position, Rifkind told reporters during a visit to the Palestinian town of Hebron: "We believe the possibility of a Palestinian state cannot be excluded."

"The British government believes all Jewish settlements in the (Arab) occupied territories are illegal and that they should not continue," he added in the West Bank town where 400 Jewish settlers live among 100,000 Palestinians.

Both remarks were likely to anger Israel's right-wing government, which has vowed to expand Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza and opposes the creation of an independent Palestinian homeland.

On a one-day visit to Israel and Palestinian areas, Rifkind also met Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in self-ruled Gaza and urged Israel and the PLO to reach a deal on implementing a long overdue partial Israeli troop pullout from Hebron.

"If we can get progress on Hebron and redeployment of Israeli forces, this will not only bring much needed relief to the people of Hebron, it will also unlock much else that needs to be done," Rifkind said at a joint news conference with Arafat.
Arafat reacted angrily to Israeli accusations of foot-dragging in talks on implementing a long overdue Israeli troop redeployment in Hebron.
"You can believe these big lies? Who can hesitate to deliver and to free the biggest city in the West Bank -- Hebron," Arafat said.

Earlier, at a joint news conference in Jerusalem with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, Rifkind said both Israel and the PLO should address the issue of Hebron "in an inspired way that recognises the great prizes to be won."
Rifkind's Hebron visit, sandwiched between talks with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, President Ezer Weizman and Arafat, was cleared with his Israeli hosts, British officials said.

Britain sees the delayed partial pullout of troops from Hebron, first postponed after a wave of Moslem militant suicide bombings last March and put on hold again after Netanyahu's election in May, as one of the key reasons for the build-up of Palestinian frustration at the slow progress towards peace.
"I think Hebron has become crucial to whether there is a future for the peace process," Rifkind said. "Without Hebron, it is rhetoric. With Hebron, it begins to look for real."

British diplomats steadfastly denied Rifkind would try to rival French President Jacques Chirac, who during a visit last week publicly turned on Israeli security men and accused them of provocation during a visit to Jerusalem's Old City and was given a hero's welcome by Palestinians.
"We work together in the European Union on this matter," Rifkind said about Middle East affairs.
Privately, London -- which wants Europe to complement rather than try to supplant the mediation efforts of the United States -- is wary of Chirac's diplomatic intentions.
Officials stressed Rifkind was determined to avoid "megaphone diplomacy" or "grandstanding" -- a word used by British newspaper commentators to describe Chirac's behaviour.
Rifkind flew into Israel from Vietnam after accompanying Queen Elizabeth on a vist to Thailand. He leaves on Monday for Abu Dhabi.
